q: Every thermometer uses a physical property that varies with temperature.
e: This varying physical property is the fundamental basis for all thermometer operations.

q: This property is referred to as the thermometric property of the thermometer.
e: The specific physical property that changes with temperature is called the thermometric property.

q: The thermometric property of a liquid-in-glass thermometer is the thermal contraction of the liquid.
e: The thermometric property of a liquid-in-glass thermometer is the thermal expansion of the liquid.

q: The liquid-in-glass thermometer consists of a thin glass bulb joined to a capillary tube with a narrow bore which is sealed at its other end.
e: This structural design allows the liquid to expand into the narrow capillary tube for measurement.

q: When the bulb becomes warmer, the liquid in it expands less than the bulb.
e: When the bulb becomes warmer, the liquid in it expands more than the bulb, forcing liquid into the capillary tube.

q: The thinner the bulb wall is, the faster the response of the thermometer will be when the temperature changes.
e: A thinner bulb wall allows for quicker heat transfer, resulting in a faster thermometer response.

q: The liquid used usually contains mercury (or) coloured alcohol.
e: Mercury and coloured alcohol are the standard liquids used in liquid-in-glass thermometers.

q: Alcohol has a higher freezing point than mercury so it is more suitable for low-temperature measurements.
e: Alcohol has a lower freezing point than mercury, making it more suitable for low-temperature measurements.

q: Thermocouple thermometers are electrical thermometers which make use of the voltage that develops when two different metals are in contact.
e: This voltage generation at the junction of two different metals is the principle behind thermocouple thermometers.

q: This voltage varies with pressure.
e: This voltage varies with temperature, not pressure.

q: One of the junctions is maintained at $0^{\circ} ext{C}$ and the other junction is used as the temperature probe.
e: Maintaining a reference junction at $0^{\circ}	ext{C}$ allows the other junction to accurately measure the target temperature.

q: The voltmeter can be calibrated directly in $^{\circ} ext{C}$.
e: The voltmeter measuring the thermocouple's voltage can be directly calibrated to display temperature in $^{\circ}	ext{C}$.

q: Because of the large size of a thermocouple junction, thermocouple thermometers are used to measure rapidly changing temperatures.
e: Because of the small size of a thermocouple junction, they are used to measure rapidly changing temperatures.

q: Thermocouple thermometers can be used to measure much lower temperatures than liquid-in-glass thermometers.
e: Thermocouple thermometers can be used to measure much higher temperatures than liquid-in-glass thermometers.

q: The voltage of a thermocouple can be measured and recorded automatically.
e: The electrical nature of the thermocouple output allows for automatic measurement and recording.

q: Resistance thermometer uses the fact that the electrical resistance of a metal (e.g platinum) wire decreases with temperature.
e: A resistance thermometer uses the fact that the electrical resistance of a metal wire increases with temperature.

q: A resistance thermometer can measure temperatures accurately in the range $-200^{\circ} ext{C}$ to $1200^{\circ} ext{C}$.
e: This wide range makes resistance thermometers highly versatile for accurate temperature measurement.

q: A resistance thermometer is best for rapidly changing temperatures.
e: A resistance thermometer is best for steady temperatures, not rapidly changing ones.

q: A resistance thermometer is small in size.
e: A resistance thermometer is bulky, not small.

q: Thermometric substances can be solids, liquids (or) gases.
e: Any state of matter can serve as a thermometric substance if it has a suitable varying physical property.

q: They have physical properties that vary continuously and linearly with temperature.
e: This continuous and linear variation is essential for accurate and predictable temperature measurement.
